title: Tangkhul Hao Ngashan: Customary Law, Clan Exogamy, and Social Governance
alternate_titles: Jurisprudence, Kinship Systems, and Conflict Resolution in Tangkhul Customary Law
journal: Tribal Jurisprudence & Cultural Bulletin of Manipur
publisher: Wung Cultural Research Forum / Directorate for Development of Tribals, Imphal
subject: Customary Law, Tribal Jurisprudence & Clan Governance
notes: Definitive codification and analysis of Tangkhul customary jurisprudence, clan exogamy, and village court administration.
abstract: Hao Ngashan embodies the unwritten constitutional and customary legal code governing Tangkhul society since time immemorial. This paper analyzes the structural pillars of Tangkhul customary jurisprudence: the patrilineal clan system (Shang), strict clan exogamy (Kashan), land tenure mechanisms, the judicial authority of the Village Council (Hangva), and traditional dispute settlement procedures. We examine the sacred oath-taking formula (Tuishot) and demonstrate how customary law operates harmoniously alongside modern constitutional protections in Manipur.

sections.title: 1. The Clan (Shang) and Exogamous Marriage (Kashan)
sections.content: Tangkhul social structure is organized into patrilineal clans (Shang) that trace their descent from common ancestors. The bedrock principle of social ethics is Kashan—strict clan exogamy. Intermarriage within the same Shang is considered an intolerable moral taboo (Kashansha) that historically incurred banishment from the village territory. All marriages must link distinct Shangs, creating enduring reciprocal obligations and alliances across the community.

tangkhul_data.notes: Fundamental marital taboo and governance rule.

sections.title: 2. The Village Court (Hangva) & Judicial Administration
sections.content: Civic, property, and criminal disputes are adjudicated by the Hangva (Village Council and Court of Elders), presided over by the hereditary Awungshi (chief). Each major clan is represented by a senior elder (Hangva-khana). The court prioritizes reconciliation (Tui-ngalung) and restitution rather than retributive punishment. Fines historically took the form of cattle, swine, woven blankets (Haora), or rice beer (Khor).

sections.title: 3. The Sacred Oath Formula: Tuishot
sections.content: When evidence in boundary or theft disputes is ambiguous and witnesses are divided, the dispute is resolved by Tuishot (the solemn oath before earth and heaven). The disputing parties bite a tiger tooth (Haram-ha) or plunge stones into sacred water, invoking divine retribution upon whoever utters falsehood. The fear of ancestral and cosmic retribution ensured near-absolute truthfulness in customary legal proceedings.

tangkhul_data.notes: Supreme evidentiary oath before spirits and earth.

tangkhul_data.notes: Symbol of wild retribution against perjury.
